content:
Friday marks the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks. Dozens of declassified presidential briefing documents that day detailed the intelligence government officials had gathered before the hijackings about Osama bin Laden and al-Qaeda — the attacks that killed nearly 3,000 people and reshaped American national security.

The documents show how security analysts tracked bin Laden's movements and support networks, as well as concerns about potential threats to American targets. They also detail officials' understanding of his networks in the United States and other countries, including how his operations were funded.

CIA Director Ratcliffe called the move an "act of extraordinary transparency," and said it was the largest single release of declassified President's Daily Briefs in the agency's history. These highly classified briefings are produced by the intelligence community for the government's top leadership.

The documents range from a February 1998 file prepared for then-President Clinton titled "Terrorists Seek Weapons of Mass Destruction Capability" — which mentioned bin Laden and other Islamic extremists — to a September 12, 2001 report, in which a source noted the attacks had been planned for two years and had also targeted the U.S. Capitol.

An April 1998 document described the Taliban's reluctance to hand over bin Laden, who was considered their "guest" in Afghanistan at the time. It noted the Taliban were "grateful for his assistance during the Soviet occupation" and therefore "did not wish to jeopardize him by monitoring or restricting his activities."

Briefers in July 1998 considered it a "reasonable assessment" that "bin Laden could be planning attacks against U.S. interests on the homeland" and noted his "interest in using chemical and biological weapons to mount attacks."

Two months later, a briefer wrote that bin Laden's "first priority was an attack on U.S. soil in Washington" and that al-Qaeda "could be expected to crash a plane loaded with explosives into an American city."

Potential hijacking operations were also discussed in December 1998, when a briefer described the plotters having "evaded security checks in a recent exercise at an undisclosed New York airport," and noted that "members of bin Laden's network had received training in hijacking."

Other documents detail bin Laden's pursuit of materials to build a "dirty bomb" — a conventional weapon infused with radioactive material. Intelligence officials noted that by June 1999, his operatives had conducted related explosive experiments to "improve their energy output."

About two years before the attacks, intelligence officials had observed that bin Laden appeared to be deceiving the Taliban, concealing his intentions to launch unprovoked attacks against the United States. Briefings prepared for President George Bush in early 2001 focused in part on bin Laden "experimenting crudely with producing and deploying biological weapons."

A report a month before the attacks noted that bin Laden was "committed to launching terrorist attacks on U.S. soil" and referenced al-Qaeda's 1998 attacks on U.S. embassies as "demonstrating he plans far ahead and does not back down in the face of setbacks."

At the time — August 2001 — officials wrote that "suspicious activity in the United States consistent with preparations for hijackings or other types of attacks, including recent surveillance of federal buildings in New York," adding that the FBI was "conducting approximately 70 full field investigations throughout the United States related to bin Laden."

Many of the documents are redacted to hide the names of sources and other identifying information. The papers do not appear to offer any new breakthroughs on the planning of the attacks or officials' understanding of the events as they unfolded.

In the years after the attacks, a bipartisan commission highlighted the lack of information-sharing between agencies such as the CIA and FBI, and made recommendations that led to the creation of new positions, including a unified Director of National Intelligence, and a National Counterterrorism Center tasked with analyzing terrorism information from across government at home and abroad.

When asked about the declassified documents, the White House pointed to another set of records released by the National Archives the same day. Those included interviews with national security officials from the Clinton and Bush administrations, the product of the 2002-2004 commission that investigated the attacks.
